stanzas.t:
turquoise rushing,
within millenia of connected disorder.

This morning holds ambivalence,
a subtle smallness,
constructed by,
cool, damp divine.

The fish are here,
the trees, the brush, the roses,
a single collective force.

From your world to mine,
your power pours into my desire
for entitled freedom

im obligated to let you go,
gasping,
life dangling between us.

on the sheen of river stones
you disappear into the malaise,
leaving my soul alone,
guilty and yearning.

properties.place: Hotel Mirador, Santa Lucía Milpas Altas, Guatemala
properties.title: Hammock Guy
properties.teaser: On comfort — the kind you chase out there, and the kind that only settles in once you stop.
properties.body:
My attempts to define comfort lately have felt like a contortion, an odd projection of insecurity.

Our PC staff showed us a graphic: someone lying in a hammock, hands behind their head, under the label “Comfort Zone.” On the other side, a person wearing a crown, flying through the air with wings and a magic wand, labeled “Magic Zone,” a strong, defining line drawn between the two.

Anytime I see a dualistic model for unpacking a complex concept, I tend to raise an eyebrow. Binary thinking not only pushes us toward fear through comparison, it's often the product of a simplistic, reductionist perspective.

Be that as it may, the question I'd pose to you, dear reader: what is real comfort?

Pausing to reflect on my own life, I'm not sure I could point to a single external source I've consistently relied on to make me feel it. Not trying to shit on hammock guy, I'd venture he did feel a real comfort resting there, gently swaying side to side, like an infant held close in a mother's arms.

But we tend to treat these external supports as proof of an internal security. If I can just find that feeling out there, I'll take it in and turn it into the safety I've been missing. And so we keep chasing, keep looking, for some person or some moment to make us feel not even better, just different.

Real comfort, the kind that courses through your veins and fills the marrow in your bones, only comes with accepting that no external source will ever give us the feeling we want most. And there's a strange freedom in that. Comfort isn't a place you arrive at. It's what settles in once you stop trying to get there.

properties.title: A Strong Base
properties.teaser: El Quince, a greased pole, and what do you do with a privilege you didn't earn?
properties.body:
The 15th of September in Guatemala is el Quince, Día de la Independencia. This day also marked one full week here in la tierra de la eterna primavera, the land of eternal spring. El Quince is long, filled with school bands marching through the streets: drums, trumpet, clarinet, saxophone, trombone, even a tuba in the bigger high school bands.

Before leaving the USA, I tried to ask myself how I was arriving to Guate. I waffled, reaching for an answer that felt honest without flattening the privilege I carry.

I have always known my body is the core privilege I arrive with. However I turn the question, how do I show up?, I return to my body. To the outward eye: six foot two, blonde hair, blue eyes, 195 pounds, tattooed in detailed art, scarred from expensive surgeries.

My body is my privilege.

Recently, in an altered state, a thought arrived unbidden, like a bubble bursting, as I walked to the river to bathe, an hour of humid mid-afternoon yoga still on my skin. I am just this body. I wanted to swat it away, I'm more than that, my ego answering fast. The thoughts swirled back and forth as I dove headfirst into a slow, winding eddy.

On el Quince I was mostly a watcher. My cohort and I walked to the stadium to see the bands perform one by one, and after lunch some of my colleagues joined the dance competitions in the town square, and the blindfolded greased-pig chase, (ask me for the video if you need a laugh). All day I felt a subtle tug to join, and stood back instead, watching, smiling, cheering, being with the people and my fellow PC members.

The last event of the day belongs to el palo ensebado. A pole had been cemented into the ground days before and lightly covered in grease. Two flags were set along the pole, one thirty feet up and the last at the top, fifty feet in the air. The goal is simple: climb, grab the flags, take the prize, 3,000 quetzales for the first flag and another 1,000 for the last. I gave in. I joined the other men and was met with cheers as I approached.

I gripped the pole and offered my body as a base, a place for other men to climb. We'd start strong, several of us holding tight while men launched onto our shoulders toward the flags. But tiredness comes fast with a grown man standing on you, and one by one they eventually would slide back down.

After an hour and a half of failed attempts, myself and the Guatemalan men climbing beside me, stood perplexed, and regrouped. I used the time to rehydrate and process with friends nearby. Suddenly another effort launched, this time without me. A man had a rope hanging loosely around his neck. He scrambled over his friends, fashioned the rope around the pole and both his legs, and over the next hour climbed the entire pole alone, grabbed both flags, and lowered himself slowly back to the ground.

I arrived at the base of el palo the same way I am arriving in Guate: with my body. I made myself a base, a place for others to stand.

This wasn't enough. The man who reached the top climbed with patience and a rope, not the brute fact of a body.

I came with what I have always counted on, and watched my efforts fall short. In the end the flags came down in another man's hands, and the whole square cheered like they were ours.

properties.place: Mirador de la Montaña de Oración, Guatemala
properties.title: The Question
properties.subtitle: conocer
properties.body:
Why are we here?

I asked in an exasperated tone to my friend, conveniently four weeks ahead of me in PC training in El Salvador. A man revs his motorcycle around the corner toward me, and I turn from the exhaust and pull up my hood to blunt the sound against my headphones.

I listen as she says, simply:

I'm here to wake up every day, learn a few new Spanish words, have fun, and meet interesting people.

I exhale out loud. I love that answer for her. There is so much beauty in the mundane.

My answer feels more complicated.

The night before, I'd been talking with my host family. My brother made a joke, a romantic suggestion between me and someone in my cohort. This has happened more than once, to me and to the people I'm here with. The first few times I laughed and shrugged and said little. This time felt different, and I found myself explaining that I am not here looking for a romantic, intimate love. That is not why I am here. I reached for the verb mantener, a clean cognate, “to maintain” my relationships with my cohort through the length of my service. Only later did I learn that mantener also means “to support.” That is closer.

The next night, over dinner, I was telling my family about my leave allowances, how I'd like to ver, to see, more of Guatemala. They corrected me: use conocer for getting to know a place, not just laying eyes on one.

Conocer is a knowledge verb, to know a place, a person, a subject. You build that knowledge by showing up, paying attention, and staying. There is no knowing without relation. The knowledge lives between you and what you have come to know, or it does not live at all. That is closest.

I think a lot about the “relationship escalator,” the pre-built idea of what a good, healthy, normal relationship is supposed to become. The escalator hands you the knowledge before you have earned any: here is what this is, here is who you are inside it, here is the next step up. I am trying to refuse that. Trying not to arrive with preconceived notions of who I am in relation to a person, a place, myself. Trying not to bring expectations to something I have not yet come to conocer.

So I am here to build knowledge the slow way. To know this land and its people the same way, by showing up. To dissolve the boundaries pressed into me that no longer nourish my mind, body, and soul, and to come to know myself with the same patience, arriving with nothing decided in advance.

This is why I am here. This will always be why I'm here.

properties.place: Peace Corps office, Santa Lucía Milpas Altas, Guatemala
properties.title: Bajo y Alto
properties.subtitle: It's all just a ride
properties.body:
Why the fuck does this feel so existential?

I ask as the belt around my waist suddenly feels five notches too tight and my heartbeat soars, as if my body is preparing to defend itself or sprint. The interview drags on.

This response is just information. Take a deep breath.

I tell myself as I watch and listen to a sworn-in PC volunteer of one year conduct a mock interview with a joven, a youth, on their understanding of life skills, mental health and relationships.

I need to get up and walk out of this room. Fresh air will help.

I ignore these thoughts. I can do this. I can sit in the discomfort of my amygdala firing, triggering my mammalian responses to a perceived threat.

The interview concludes, my cohort members and I are dismissed for lunch, and I'm still simmering. I have to put some words to my feelings. I need to actually feel. I quickly scribble onto my notepad:

How am I supposed to make someone feel safe sharing with me when I have no idea what they're communicating?

I don't feel like I can, and that upsets me.

I'm now at a roaring, uneven boil and the tears are here. They spill out with a child-like fear that I cannot control how I'm showing up, all because of my lack of Spanish comprehension.

I am hesitant to define the term masculinity. Not only my definition, my embodiment of masculinity is different from yours, dear reader. Regardless of your biology, we all contain multitudes of the “normal” expression of any and all genders. (Let's also breathe some space into the notion that any attempt at defining and characterizing a group of people's behavior based on their biology is inherently limiting, controlling and a vain attempt at reducing people to predictable patterns wherein we can perceive our individual position within a self/societally constructed hierarchy that reproduces inequality, enforces power dynamics and creates our own, limiting beliefs).

A definition of masculinity I feel comfortable embracing is one in which I am able to create safe spaces for the people I care about to express and be themselves authentically, without judgement.

So watching an experienced, well-spoken (in Spanish) PC volunteer show exactly how to build those spaces, in the cultural context I'm still adjusting to, should have been an inspiring experience, right?

Wrong.

During those 15 minutes, I realized that I do not have the skills to show up for the people here in the ways I have come to define myself by.

I've had the privilege to comprehend and construct my own life path (remember, I'm the map guy?). I've been able to see how X+Y=Z. My experience here in Guate is one of very few situations in my life where I cannot see clearly: (X) where I am now, (Y) the work I need to put in to get (Z) the result I desire. And that is scary as hell.

properties.title: Five Quetzales
properties.subtitle: Why does it all have to be so complicated?
properties.teaser: A locked gym, an old man with a cane, and five quetzales I didn’t want to spend.
properties.body:
Just keep walking…

I tell myself as the staggered voice of the old man competes with the sound of my noise-cancelling earbuds.

I arrive at the gym and look down at my phone, it’s 0745. The exact time the volunteer I’m visiting here in Pologuá, Levi (name changed for anonymity), and I had agreed to meet. The door’s locked, Levi isn’t here, and I am not sensing any movement inside.

I turn back toward the street and let out a sigh.

Maybe he’s already inside and I just can’t hear him?

My gaze wanders down the street, toward the municipal building and the modest town square in front. A gesture catches my eye. It’s the old man again, waving one of his canes and, I presume, still talking to me, since I’m the only other person around, even though I’m at least 100m away.

Even if I did talk to him, there’s no way I’d be able to understand him.

These thoughts move in and out of my recently awakened brain while I’m also trying to listen to one of my favorite podcasts on relationship anarchy. Insightful and inspiring but complex and nuanced, I’m trying to hang onto every word.

I turn back to face the gym with my phone unlocked, about to text Levi, Buenos días! I’m out in front of the gym. As I’m deciding how annoying this message is to send to someone now three minutes late, I look up and see Levi striding across the street, heading toward the old man.

He spends about five minutes with him, visiting, then makes his way over to me with a subtle smile, and we proceed to exercise for an hour.

After finishing, Levi turns to me as we walk out of the gym.

“Do you have 5 quetzales? We should give it to that old man. He can’t really walk and he needs to take a tuk tuk ride somewhere.”

I respond, simply, “Yes.” We walk over and give the old man five quetzales, excusing ourselves after a few minutes of mindless chatter where he goes on about the chuchos (the stray dogs in the street) and even offers a name for one or two he claims to have a relationship with.

Walking towards breakfast, I’m feeling a subtle sense of ambivalence. I’m still adjusting to my new budget here in Guate, living on a modest allowance, and this old man can’t walk and needs to pay for a tuk tuk. I walked right past him first thing this morning, and now I’m handing him a 5q bill.

Why does it all have to be so complicated?

“Arriving in Pologuá, I was not exactly a smitten kitten.”

Levi told me and another trainee I was traveling with the night before, over dinner. I can see why. This place is not, at first glance, aesthetically beautiful. It’s a small community where the highway splits in two directions toward much larger cities, one toward Huehuetenango, the other toward Momostenango. The ambiance of passing trucks and buses vibrates off of the concrete buildings. Walking through the streets, you’re often stepping over plastic bottles, empty bags of chips, and other discarded single-use items.

There are three main streets and one open-air market where people can get fresh produce, meat, clothes, whatever they need. The municipal building sits at the north end of town, and when I say there’s a modest town square in front, modest is generous. A fountain with no water, crumbling concrete steps, a few benches. Over the loudspeaker during the three days I visited was an ad for a traveling doctor passing through town.

No coffee shops, no real sit-down restaurants, no green spaces, no bodies of water to leisurely watch the day go by. This place has not gotten the memo on 21st century urban planning. And yet, there is so much love here.

I don’t need to understand every word I hear in Spanish as I’m offered a night time car ride back to my hotel by Levi’s host brother and sister. I can’t remember the last hot shower my body actually fit under, but I can see the twinkle in Mama Javina’s eyes, Levi’s host mom, as she hands me a bowl of homemade chicken soup and says Buen provecho! In my hotel room with two broken window panes, I shiver as my feet stick out of the two wool comforters (Pologuá sits over 9000 ft above sea level, nights are cold). The next morning I’m warmed by the immediate embrace and laughter of children at the local primaria.

I am always able to recognize love when I see it. But I am quick to judge first, the outward appearance of a person, a place. This is only fear, the nervous system reaching for safety, projecting out the past as an assured future, all while missing the present.

Outward appearance will never be a condition for love. A place with no water in its fountain, a language I can’t follow, an old man I’ll never understand, all of these worked to keep my heart closed. That is all fear is: deciding, in the dark, to stay shut.

So what is this universe? Just a ride that we can change anytime. No effort, no work, no money. A choice, right now, between fear and love.
